items.stem: In an investigation of how the period of a pendulum depends on its length, the length is the …
items.answer: independent variable
items.markingKey: The quantity deliberately changed.

items.stem: Explain why a range of at least six values of the independent variable is used in an investigation.
items.answer: Enough points are needed to establish the trend and draw a reliable best-fit line; spreading them over a wide range shows whether the relationship holds and reduces the effect of uncertainty on the gradient.
items.markingKey: enough points for a reliable line/trend [1]; wide range [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a data-logger may be better than a stopwatch for measuring a rapidly changing p.d.
items.answer: A data-logger takes readings at precise short intervals without human reaction time, so it can record changes too fast to read by eye.
items.markingKey: many readings at short intervals [1]; no reaction-time error [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe plans an experiment to investigate how the e.m.f. E induced in a small search coil depends on the frequency f of the alternating current in a solenoid. Which is the independent variable?
items.answer: frequency f
items.markingKey: Independent: frequency f; dependent: peak induced e.m.f. E.

items.stem: Yusuf plans an experiment to investigate how the time t½ for the p.d. across a discharging capacitor to halve depends on the resistance R in the circuit. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and one variable that should be controlled.
items.answer: Independent: resistance R; dependent: time t½ for the p.d. to halve; control: the same capacitor and the same initial charging voltage.
items.markingKey: independent [1]; dependent [1]; control variable [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara is asked to plan an investigation into how the resistance R of a thermistor depends on its thermodynamic temperature T, given that R = R₀e^(b/T). It is suggested that the relationship is ln R = ln R₀ + b/T. (Paper 5 planning) (a) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (b) Explain how the data are analysed.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature T; dependent: resistance R. (b) Plot ln R against 1/T; the relationship is valid if it is a straight line; gradient = b.
items.markingKey: (a) Independent: temperature T; dependent: resistance R [1] (b) graph [1]; validity check [1]; constant from gradient [1] [3]

items.stem: In a planning question, a control variable is one that …
options: is kept constant so that it does not affect the dependent variable
is measured to find the result
items.answer: is kept constant so that it does not affect the dependent variable
items.markingKey: Fair test.

items.stem: Explain the importance of a safety precaution in an investigation using a radioactive source.
items.answer: Ionising radiation can damage cells; using tongs, keeping a distance and limiting exposure time reduce the dose received.
items.markingKey: radiation hazard to cells [1]; precaution reduces dose [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a student should check that a relationship is linear before extracting a constant from the gradient.
items.answer: If the points do not lie on a straight line within their uncertainties the assumed relationship is not supported, so a gradient would not give a valid constant.
items.markingKey: linearity tests the relationship [1]; gradient only meaningful if linear [1] [2]

items.stem: An experiment is planned to investigate how the amplitude A of a pendulum decreases with the number n of oscillations when a card is attached to the bob, given A = A₀e^(−kn). Explain how the data should be analysed to test the relationship ln A = ln A₀ − kn.
items.answer: Plot ln A against n; a straight line confirms the relationship; gradient = −k.
items.markingKey: plot ln A against n [1]; straight line test and gradient = −k [1]; how the constant is found from the gradient or intercept [1] [3]

items.stem: Ravi plans an experiment to investigate how the frequency f of a vibrating wire depends on the tension T in the wire. Which is the independent variable?
items.answer: tension T
items.markingKey: Independent: tension T; dependent: frequency f of the fundamental.

items.stem: Leila plans an experiment to investigate how the e.m.f. E induced in a small search coil depends on the frequency f of the alternating current in a solenoid. Which is the independent variable?
items.answer: frequency f
items.markingKey: Independent: frequency f; dependent: peak induced e.m.f. E.

items.stem: Omar plans an experiment to investigate how the time constant of an RC circuit depends on the capacitance C, given V = V₀e^(−t/RC). (a) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (b) Describe how the dependent variable should be measured. (c) State one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) independent: capacitance C; dependent: time constant τ (b) record V against t with a data-logger for each capacitor; find τ as −1/gradient of ln V against t (c) keep the charging p.d. low and discharge capacitors before handling
items.markingKey: (a) both variables [1] (b) method [1]; detail improving accuracy [1] (c) relevant precaution [1] [4]

items.stem: Ana is asked to plan an investigation into how the frequency f of a vibrating wire depends on the tension T in the wire. It is suggested that the relationship is f = (1/2L)√(T/μ). (Paper 5 planning) (a) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (b) State the key variable to be controlled and how it is controlled. (c) Suggest one additional detail to improve the accuracy.
items.answer: (a) Independent: tension T; dependent: frequency f of the fundamental. (b) The same wire (mass per unit length) and the same vibrating length. (c) Repeat readings and average; use a wide range of values; check for zero errors.
items.markingKey: (a) Independent: tension T; dependent: frequency f of the fundamental [1] (b) The same wire (mass per unit length) and the same vibrating length [1] (c) Repeat readings and average; use a wide range of values; check for zero errors [1]

items.stem: Samuel is asked to plan an investigation into how the amplitude A of a pendulum decreases with the number n of oscillations when a card is attached to the bob, given A = A₀e^(−kn). It is suggested that the relationship is ln A = ln A₀ − kn. (Paper 5 planning) (a) Describe the method of data collection, including the instruments used. (b) State one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) Measure A against a scale behind the pendulum, viewed at eye level to avoid parallax (or video and step through frames). (b) Ensure the stand is clamped so that it does not topple.
items.markingKey: (a) how independent variable varied/measured [1]; how dependent variable measured [1]; additional detail [1] [3] (b) Ensure the stand is clamped so that it does not topple [1]

items.stem: A quantity y is thought to depend on x according to y = axⁿ. Which graph gives a straight line?
options: y against xⁿ with n unknown
items.answer: lg y against lg x
items.markingKey: lg y = n lg x + lg a.

items.stem: Explain why taking logarithms of both sides of y = axⁿ allows n to be found from a graph.
items.answer: lg y = n lg x + lg a has the form Y = mX + c, so a graph of lg y against lg x is a straight line with gradient n and intercept lg a.
items.markingKey: log equation in straight-line form [1]; gradient n, intercept lg a [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why natural logarithms are used for exponential relationships such as A = A₀e^(−λt).
items.answer: ln(e^(−λt)) = −λt, so ln A = ln A₀ − λt is linear in t with gradient −λ directly.
items.markingKey: ln of exponential gives linear term [1]; gradient −λ [1] [2]

items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship y = axⁿ using a straight-line graph. Which graph should be plotted?
items.answer: lg y against lg x
items.markingKey: Plot lg y against lg x: gradient n, y-intercept lg a.

items.stem: It is suggested that two quantities are related by F = k/dⁿ, where the other symbols are constants. A graph is plotted to test this. State the quantities to plot on each axis and give expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept.
items.answer: y-axis lg F, x-axis lg d; gradient = −n; y-intercept = lg k
items.markingKey: axes [1]; gradient = −n [1]; intercept = lg k [1] [3]

items.stem: It is suggested that two quantities are related by A = A₀e^(−λt), where the other symbols are constants. A graph is plotted to test this. State the quantities to plot on each axis and give expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept. Explain how you would decide whether the relationship is valid.
items.answer: y-axis ln A, x-axis t; gradient = −λ; y-intercept = ln A₀; valid if the points lie on a straight line within their error bars
items.markingKey: axes [1]; gradient = −λ [1]; intercept = ln A₀ [1]; straight line within error bars [1] [4]

items.stem: A student investigates how the terminal speed v of a sphere falling in a liquid depends on its radius r. It is suggested that v = kr^n. (a) Explain why a graph of lg v against lg r should be plotted. (b) For r = 4.0 mm, v = 1.6 cm s⁻¹. Calculate lg r and lg v, to 3 s.f. (c) Suggest why logarithmic scales are useful when the data span a wide range.
items.answer: (a) lg v = n lg r + lg k: straight line with gradient n and intercept lg k. (b) lg r = 0.602; lg v = 0.204 (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision.
items.markingKey: (a) log form [1]; gradient n, intercept lg k [1] [2] (b) lg r = 0.602; lg v = 0.204 [1] (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision [1]

items.stem: A student investigates how the terminal speed v of a sphere falling in a liquid depends on its radius r. It is suggested that v = kr^n. (a) Explain why a graph of lg v against lg r should be plotted. (b) Determine k, with its unit. (c) Suggest why logarithmic scales are useful when the data span a wide range.
items.answer: (a) lg v = n lg r + lg k: straight line with gradient n and intercept lg k. (b) k = 1.6 cm s⁻¹ mm^(−0.50) (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision.
items.markingKey: (a) log form [1]; gradient n, intercept lg k [1] [2] (b) k = v/rⁿ at a point [1]; value with unit [1] [2] (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the quantity given by the y-intercept of a graph of lg y against lg x for y = axⁿ. (b) The graph of lg y against lg x is a straight line with gradient 1.5 and y-intercept 0.30. What is the relationship?
Explain why the y-intercept of a lg–lg graph often cannot be read directly from the graph.
items.answer: The x-axis values of lg x on the plotted range often do not include lg x = 0, so the intercept must be calculated from y = mx + c using a point on the line and the gradient.
items.markingKey: lg x = 0 not on axis range [1]; calculate c from a point and gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship I = I₀e^(−μx) using a straight-line graph. Which graph should be plotted?
items.answer: ln I against x
items.markingKey: Plot ln I against x: gradient −μ, y-intercept ln I₀.

items.stem: A student obtains these results: x = 1.0, y = 1.2; x = 2.0, y = 0.60; x = 3.0, y = 0.400; x = 4.0, y = 0.30; x = 5.0, y = 0.24. It is suggested that y = axⁿ. (a) Calculate lg x and lg y for the first and last results. (b) Determine the gradient of a graph of lg y against lg x. (c) Hence find n and a.
items.markingKey: (a) logs to 3 d.p. or s.f. [1] (b) gradient from large triangle = −1.00 [1] (c) n = gradient [1]; lg a = lg y − n lg x, a = 1.2 [1] [4]

items.stem: Data from an experiment (t / s, (θ − θ_room) / K): t = 0, (θ − θ_room) = 70; t = 120, (θ − θ_room) = 53.6; t = 240, (θ − θ_room) = 41.1; t = 360, (θ − θ_room) = 31.5; t = 480, (θ − θ_room) = 24.1; t = 600, (θ − θ_room) = 18.5. (a) Explain why a graph of the natural logarithm of the second quantity against the first should be a straight line. (b) Determine the gradient of this graph. (c) The excess temperature is given by θ = θ₀e^(−t/τ). Determine τ.
items.answer: (a) exponential decay y = y₀e^(−kx) gives ln y = ln y₀ − kx (b) −2.22 × 10⁻³ (in units of s⁻¹) τ = 450 s
items.markingKey: (a) ln y = ln y₀ − kx linear [1] (b) ln values [1]; gradient = −2.22 × 10⁻³ [1] (c) τ = −1/gradient [1]; = 450 s [1] [5]

items.stem: A student obtains these results: x = 2.0, y = 2.0; x = 4.0, y = 8.0; x = 6.0, y = 18; x = 8.0, y = 32; x = 10, y = 50. It is suggested that y = axⁿ. items.markingKey: (a) logs to 3 d.p. or s.f. [1] (b) gradient from large triangle = 2.0 [1] (c) n = gradient [1]; lg a = lg y − n lg x, a = 0.50 [1] [4]

items.stem: Data from an experiment (x / cm, C / counts min⁻¹): x = 0, C = 800; x = 1, C = 462; x = 2, C = 266; x = 3, C = 154; x = 4, C = 88.6; x = 5, C = 51.1. (a) Explain why a graph of the natural logarithm of the second quantity against the first should be a straight line. (b) Determine the gradient of this graph. (c) Determine the linear attenuation coefficient μ and the half-value thickness.
items.answer: (a) exponential decay y = y₀e^(−kx) gives ln y = ln y₀ − kx (b) −5.50 × 10⁻¹ (in units of cm⁻¹) μ = 0.55 cm⁻¹; half-value thickness = 1.26 cm
items.markingKey: (a) ln y = ln y₀ − kx linear [1] (b) ln values [1]; gradient = −5.50 × 10⁻¹ [1] (c) μ = −gradient [1]; x½ = ln 2/μ = 1.26 cm [1] [5]

items.stem: A worst acceptable straight line is drawn …
options: through the error bars with the steepest or shallowest gradient that still fits the data
through the first and last points only
items.answer: through the error bars with the steepest or shallowest gradient that still fits the data
items.markingKey: Used with the best-fit line to find the uncertainty in the gradient.

items.stem: Explain how error bars and a worst acceptable line are used to find the uncertainty in a gradient.
items.answer: Plot error bars for each point; draw the best-fit line and the steepest (or shallowest) straight line that passes through all the error bars; the uncertainty is the difference between their gradients.
items.markingKey: error bars and worst line through them [1]; uncertainty = difference in gradients [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the uncertainty in ln y is Δy/y rather than ln(Δy).
items.answer: For small changes, d(ln y) = dy/y, so an absolute uncertainty Δy in y produces an uncertainty Δy/y in ln y; ln(Δy) has no meaning as an uncertainty.
items.markingKey: d(ln y)/dy = 1/y [1]; Δ(ln y) = Δy/y [1] [2]

items.stem: In an experiment to test T² = (4π²/g)l, using a graph of T²/s² against l/m, the best-fit line has gradient 4.05 s² m⁻¹ and the worst acceptable line has gradient 3.85 s² m⁻¹. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the gradient.
items.markingKey: |3.85 − 4.05|/4.05 × 100 = 5.0%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In an experiment to test V = E − Ir, using a graph of V/V against I/A (magnitude of gradient = r), the best-fit line has gradient 0.85 Ω and the worst acceptable line has gradient 0.799 Ω. Calculate the absolute and percentage uncertainties in the gradient.
items.markingKey: absolute = |difference| = 0.051 Ω [1]; ÷ best gradient [1]; × 100 = 6.0% [1] [3]

items.stem: In a Paper 5 analysis, a graph of ln(V/V) against t/s is plotted with error bars. The best-fit line has gradient −0.046 s⁻¹ and y-intercept 2.5. The worst acceptable line has gradient −0.0483 s⁻¹ and y-intercept 2.58. (a) Explain how the worst acceptable line is drawn. (b) Determine the uncertainty in the gradient. (c) The relationship is V = V₀e^(−t/RC). Determine RC and its absolute uncertainty.
items.answer: (a) Steepest or shallowest straight line passing through all the error bars. (b) ± 0.0023 s⁻¹ (c) RC = 21.7 ± 1.0 s
items.markingKey: (a) Steepest or shallowest straight line passing through all the error bars [1] (b) ± 0.0023 s⁻¹ [1] (c) RC = −1/gradient [1]; uncertainty [1] [2]

items.stem: The best-fit line has gradient 2.40 and the worst acceptable line has gradient 2.55. What is the absolute uncertainty in the gradient?
Explain how the uncertainty in the y-intercept can be found from a graph.
items.answer: Find the intercept of the worst acceptable line (calculated using its gradient and a point on it); the uncertainty is the difference between this and the best-fit intercept.
items.markingKey: intercept of worst line [1]; difference from best intercept [1] [2]

items.stem: A measured value is 2.5 ± 0.10. Calculate the absolute uncertainty in ln of this value.
items.markingKey: Δ(ln x) = Δx/x = 0.10/2.5 = 0.040. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An experimental value of g is 9.6 ± 0.3 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.81 m s⁻². Which conclusion is correct?
options: the result disagrees with the accepted value
the result proves the accepted value is wrong
the result agrees with the accepted value within the uncertainty
items.answer: the result agrees with the accepted value within the uncertainty
items.markingKey: 9.81 lies within 9.3–9.9.

items.stem: Which change most improves the reliability of a set of results?
items.answer: repeating readings and calculating means
items.markingKey: Reduces the effect of random errors and reveals anomalies.

items.stem: Explain how a student should decide whether an experimental value supports a theoretical prediction.
items.answer: Calculate the uncertainty in the experimental value; if the predicted value lies within the range value ± uncertainty, the result supports the prediction; if not, there may be a systematic error or the theory may not apply.
items.markingKey: compare using uncertainty range [1]; conclusion if within/outside [1] [2]

items.stem: A student determines the speed of sound in air as 320 ± 13 m s⁻¹. The accepted value is 340 m s⁻¹. The result is
options: not consistent with the accepted value
impossible to judge without a graph
items.answer: not consistent with the accepted value
items.markingKey: Range 307 to 332; accepted value outside this range.

items.stem: A student tests the prediction that the gradient of a graph should equal 2.0. The best-fit gradient is 2.31 and the worst acceptable gradient is 2.36. (a) State whether the result supports the prediction, explaining your answer. (b) Explain why a straight line not passing through the origin may still support a linear relationship.
items.answer: (a) No: the predicted value is outside 2.31 ± 0.050. (b) It shows y = mx + c with a constant offset, perhaps from a systematic error; the gradient may still be valid.
items.markingKey: (a) comparison with range [1]; conclusion [1] [2] (b) It shows y = mx + c with a constant offset, perhaps from a systematic error; the gradient may still be valid [1]

items.stem: A systematic error in a set of measurements …
options: shifts all readings in the same direction by a similar amount
causes random scatter about the true value
items.answer: shifts all readings in the same direction by a similar amount
items.markingKey: E.g. a zero error.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the accuracy and the precision of a result.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value; precision is how close repeated readings are to each other (small spread), regardless of whether they are close to the true value.
items.markingKey: accuracy: close to true value [1]; precision: small spread [1] [2]

items.stem: A student determines the Planck constant h as 6.43 × 10⁻³⁴ ± 1.3 × 10⁻³⁵ J s. The accepted value is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Calculate the percentage difference from the accepted value and state, with a reason, whether the result agrees with it.

items.stem: A student wants to find how the count rate from a γ source depends on the thickness of an absorber. What must be measured first and then subtracted?
options: the dead time of the counter
items.answer: the background count rate
items.markingKey: Background radiation adds to every reading.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a student should check that a relationship is linear before extracting a constant from the gradient. (b) Explain why a data-logger may be better than a stopwatch for measuring a rapidly changing p.d.
items.answer: (a) If the points do not lie on a straight line within their uncertainties the assumed relationship is not supported, so a gradient would not give a valid constant. (b) A data-logger takes readings at precise short intervals without human reaction time, so it can record changes too fast to read by eye.
items.markingKey: (a) linearity tests the relationship [1]; gradient only meaningful if linear [1] [2] (b) many readings at short intervals [1]; no reaction-time error [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya plans an experiment to investigate how the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons from a metal depends on the frequency f of the incident light. Which is the independent variable?

items.stem: Mohammed plans an experiment to investigate how the force F between two magnets depends on their separation d, given F = k/dⁿ. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and one variable that should be controlled.

items.markingKey: independent [1]; dependent [1]; control variable [1] [3]

items.stem: Ravi is asked to plan an investigation into how the e.m.f. E induced in a small search coil depends on the frequency f of the alternating current in a solenoid. It is suggested that the relationship is E ∝ f. (Paper 5 planning) (a) Explain how the data are analysed. (b) State one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) Plot E against f; the relationship is valid if it is a straight line; gradient = constant of proportionality. (b) Avoid touching the solenoid which may become hot.
items.markingKey: (a) graph [1]; validity check [1]; constant from gradient [1] [3] (b) Avoid touching the solenoid which may become hot [1]

items.stem: A capacitor discharges according to V = V₀e^(−t/RC). A graph of ln V against t has gradient …
items.answer: −1/RC
items.markingKey: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why taking logarithms of both sides of y = axⁿ allows n to be found from a graph. (b) Explain why natural logarithms are used for exponential relationships such as A = A₀e^(−λt).
items.answer: (a) lg y = n lg x + lg a has the form Y = mX + c, so a graph of lg y against lg x is a straight line with gradient n and intercept lg a. (b) ln(e^(−λt)) = −λt, so ln A = ln A₀ − λt is linear in t with gradient −λ directly.
items.markingKey: (a) log equation in straight-line form [1]; gradient n, intercept lg a [1] [2] (b) ln of exponential gives linear term [1]; gradient −λ [1] [2]

items.stem: A student investigates how the terminal speed v of a sphere falling in a liquid depends on its radius r. It is suggested that v = kr^n. (a) For r = 4.0 mm, v = 25.6 cm s⁻¹. Calculate lg r and lg v, to 3 s.f. (b) For r = 1.0 mm, v = 1.6 cm s⁻¹. Use this and the previous point to find n. (c) Suggest why logarithmic scales are useful when the data span a wide range.
items.answer: (a) lg r = 0.602; lg v = 1.41 (b) n = 2.0 (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision.
items.markingKey: (a) lg r = 0.602; lg v = 1.41 [1] (b) gradient = Δlg v/Δlg r [1]; value of n [1] [2] (c) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision [1]

items.stem: A student investigates how the terminal speed v of a sphere falling in a liquid depends on its radius r. It is suggested that v = kr^n. items.answer: (a) lg v = n lg r + lg k: straight line with gradient n and intercept lg k. (b) lg r = 0.602; lg v = 1.41 (c) n = 2.0 (d) They compress the range so all points can be plotted with useful precision.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A value of y is 25 ± 1. What is the absolute uncertainty in lg y? (b) A period T is measured as 2.00 ± 0.02 s. What is the percentage uncertainty in T²?
items.markingKey: (a) Δ(lg y) = 0.434 × Δy/y = 0.434 × 0.04. (b) Double the percentage uncertainty in T (1%).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how error bars and a worst acceptable line are used to find the uncertainty in a gradient. (b) Explain how the uncertainty in the y-intercept can be found from a graph.
items.answer: (a) Plot error bars for each point; draw the best-fit line and the steepest (or shallowest) straight line that passes through all the error bars; the uncertainty is the difference between their gradients. (b) Find the intercept of the worst acceptable line (calculated using its gradient and a point on it); the uncertainty is the difference between this and the best-fit intercept.
items.markingKey: (a) error bars and worst line through them [1]; uncertainty = difference in gradients [1] [2] (b) intercept of worst line [1]; difference from best intercept [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a risk assessment is part of planning an experiment.
items.answer: It identifies hazards (e.g. hot liquids, radiation, high voltage, falling masses) and specifies precautions to reduce the risk of harm before the experiment is carried out.

items.stem: Explain why a graph with a straight line through the origin is stronger evidence for proportionality than two calculated ratios that agree.
items.answer: A graph uses many readings over a range and shows any trend or curvature; two ratios could agree by chance and give no information about intermediate values or systematic errors.
items.markingKey: many points over a range [1]; two ratios could agree by chance [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how error bars and a worst acceptable line are used to find the uncertainty in a gradient. (b) Explain why the uncertainty in ln y is Δy/y rather than ln(Δy).
items.answer: (a) Plot error bars for each point; draw the best-fit line and the steepest (or shallowest) straight line that passes through all the error bars; the uncertainty is the difference between their gradients. (b) For small changes, d(ln y) = dy/y, so an absolute uncertainty Δy in y produces an uncertainty Δy/y in ln y; ln(Δy) has no meaning as an uncertainty.
items.markingKey: (a) error bars and worst line through them [1]; uncertainty = difference in gradients [1] [2] (b) d(ln y)/dy = 1/y [1]; Δ(ln y) = Δy/y [1] [2]
